Google Cloud SQL

Source: vignettes/cloud-sql.Rmd
cloud-sql.Rmd

Google Cloud SQL hosts PostgreSQL databases. With IAM database authentication, visitors can sign in to your Shiny app with their Google account and query the database using their own SQL permissions.

oauth_db_cloud_sql_postgres() opens native DBI connections using the visitor’s access token as the database password. shinyOAuth handles browser sign-in and token renewal. The app doesn’t need a Google service account or Application Default Credentials.

Set up access

Ask your administrator to enable IAM database authentication on the instance, add the intended IAM users or groups, and grant Cloud SQL Instance User (roles/cloudsql.instanceUser). They must also grant database privileges, such as permission to connect to reporting and read its tables. IAM login permission alone doesn’t grant access to data.

Google documents these steps in its PostgreSQL IAM login guide. This package’s Cloud SQL helper supports PostgreSQL. MySQL support is deferred pending driver validation, and Cloud SQL for SQL Server doesn’t provide this IAM database login path.

Register a Web application OAuth client in Google Cloud, configure its consent screen and register http://localhost:8100 as an authorized redirect URI. Use an internal audience for a Workspace organization when appropriate; external apps may need test users or Google’s verification process. See Google’s Web server OAuth setup. Save the client ID and secret in your local .Renviron, then restart R:

OAUTHDB_CLIENT_ID=your-google-client-id
OAUTHDB_CLIENT_SECRET=your-google-client-secret

The sign-in preset requests openid, email, and https://www.googleapis.com/auth/sqlservice.login. It doesn’t request Cloud SQL administration. Keep this Google client separate from clients requesting permissions for other data platforms.

Install RPostgres linked to libpq 16 or later.

Configure the network and certificates

The app host needs a direct route to the instance: an authorized public IP, or access to its private network. These helpers enforce server identity verification, so use a hostname matching the database’s server certificate and a trusted CA bundle.

Value Where to find it
host The DNS name in the instance’s server certificate; configure DNS so the app host can resolve it
dbname A database created on the Cloud SQL instance
user The signed-in IAM user’s full email address
sslrootcert The CA bundle for the instance’s server certificate
Client certificate and key The instance’s client certificate settings, if required

Shared and customer-managed server CAs support DNS-based identity verification. With a per-instance CA, Google restricts DNS-based verification to instances configured with Private Service Connect. Choose an instance configuration with a matching certificate name; entering an ordinary instance IP as host won’t work if that IP isn’t in its certificate. See Google’s PostgreSQL TLS setup.

PostgreSQL also accepts hostaddr when you need to connect to an IP while checking the certificate against the DNS name in host. It still requires that name to match the certificate.

A complete PostgreSQL app

Save this as example.R. Replace the hostname, database and CA file path with your instance’s settings. The username function reads the email from the selected sign-in’s validated identity, so switching accounts also changes the database username.

After signing in, click Load rows. The app starts its workers once and stops them at shutdown.

library(shiny)
library(shinyOAuth)
library(shinyOAuthDB)

client <- oauth_db_cloud_sql_client(
  client_id = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_ID"),
  client_secret = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_SECRET"),
  redirect_uri = "http://localhost:8100"
)

ui <- oauth_ui(
  fluidPage(
    actionButton("login", "Sign in"),
    actionButton("logout", "Sign out"),

    actionButton("load", "Load rows"),
    tableOutput("rows")
  ),

  id = "auth",
  client = client
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  auth <- oauth_module_server(
    "auth",
    client,
    auto_redirect = FALSE,
    async = TRUE
  )

  observeEvent(input$login, auth$request_login())
  observeEvent(input$logout, auth$logout())

  database_user <- function() {
    reference <- req(auth$connection())
    identity <- reference$identity(claims = "email")
    req(identity$id_token_claims$email)
  }

  con <- oauth_db_cloud_sql_postgres(
    auth$connection,
    host = "db.example.org",
    dbname = "reporting",
    user = database_user,
    sslrootcert = "path/to/server-ca.pem"
  )

  query_task <- oauth_db_task(con)

  observeEvent(input$load, {
    query_task$invoke("SELECT current_user AS database_user")
  })

  output$rows <- renderTable(query_task$result())
}

runApp(
  shinyApp(ui, server, uiPattern = ".*", onStart = function() {
    mirai::daemons(2)

    onStop(function() mirai::daemons(0))
  }),
  port = 8100,
  launch.browser = FALSE
)

# Open the app in your regular browser at its registered redirect URI.

Sign in to see your PostgreSQL username. To read a table, replace the query with SELECT * FROM reporting.orders LIMIT 20, using your own table name. The database enforces that user’s grants and any row policies. Use DBI parameter binding for values entered by visitors.

Connection lifetime and other settings

Create the helper inside server() and resolve connection <- con() before each query. Ordinary token renewal doesn’t rerun completed reactive queries. On the next access after the token changes, the helper replaces the connection so reconnection uses current credentials. Finish a transaction on the connection that started it. Account changes, loss of required permissions, sign-out and session end close the connection. A retained native handle isn’t a substitute for calling con().

For instances requiring client certificates, supply sslcert and sslkey together. Leave PGSERVICE and PGSERVICEFILE unset. Authentication and TLS settings cannot be changed through ....

The default required_scopes checks Cloud SQL login permission in the authorization. For a custom Google client using an alternative accepted scope, set required_scopes to match that client’s granted scopes. The database still validates the access token and IAM permissions.

These helpers implement Google’s manual IAM database authentication. A shared Cloud SQL Auth Proxy started with --auto-iam-authn signs in as the account that runs the proxy; it doesn’t select a different identity for each Shiny visitor. This guide uses direct TLS connections. The package doesn’t start or configure a proxy.
